```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.height = 3.5)

# Several data sets in this package have the same names as data sets in the
# survival package (for example `myeloma`), and the package that was attached
# last is the one that is found first. Refer to this package explicitly so that
# the examples below do not depend on the order in which packages are attached.
myeloma <- sta310::myeloma
```

```{r}
library(sta310)
```

## Overview

`sta310` contains two things that are useful when working through the
STA310 course in survival analysis at the University of Gothenburg:

* the 33 data sets that accompany Collett (2023), *Modelling Survival Data in
  Medical Research* (4th edition), documented with the background of each study
  and the coded variables; and
* a small set of teaching functions that implement the estimators from the
  lectures from first principles, so that every step in the calculation can be
  inspected rather than hidden inside a black box.

The teaching functions are not meant to replace the established implementations
in `survival` and related packages. On the contrary, most of them agree with
`survival` to within numerical tolerance, and the exercises compare the two.

## The data sets

All data sets are available by name once the package is loaded, and each of them
has a help page with the study background, the variable codings and references
to the relevant chapter and examples in Collett (2023).

```{r}
data(package = "sta310")$results[, "Item"]
```

The data sets used most often in the lectures are `iud`, `breast`, `myeloma`,
`ovarian`, `liver` and `rats`. As an example, `iud` holds the time to
discontinuation of the use of an IUD for 18 women:

```{r}
iud
```

## The Kaplan-Meier estimator

`km_estimate()` performs the product-limit calculation directly and returns the
risk set, the number of events and censorings, the survivor function and the
Greenwood standard error at every event time:

```{r}
km <- km_estimate(iud$time, iud$status)
km
```

The result agrees with `survival::survfit()` at the event times:

```{r}
sf <- survival::survfit(survival::Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = iud)
cbind(
  km_estimate = km$survival[-1],
  survfit = unname(sf$surv[sf$n.event > 0])
)
```

`km_estimate()` follows the `conf.type` argument of `survfit()`: `conf_type`
selects the scale of the confidence interval, and `truncate = FALSE` shows the
raw Wald interval, which for small samples leaves the interval `[0, 1]`:

```{r}
km_estimate(iud$time, iud$status, conf_type = "plain", truncate = FALSE)
```

`plot_km()` draws the estimate as a step function with an optional confidence
band and requires ggplot2:

```{r km-plot, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)}
plot_km(km)
```

## Cox regression fitted from first principles

`cox_fit()` maximises the partial likelihood with Newton-Raphson and handles
tied event times with the Breslow or Efron approximation. Factors have to be
expanded before the call, and the intercept column must be dropped, because a
Cox model has no intercept:

```{r}
fit <- cox_fit(myeloma$time, myeloma$status, myeloma[, c("age", "bun")])
fit
```

```{r}
x <- stats::model.matrix(~ factor(group), data = bmt_leukaemia)[, -1, drop = FALSE]
cox_fit(bmt_leukaemia$time, bmt_leukaemia$status, x)
```

The coefficients, standard errors and log-likelihood agree with
`survival::coxph()`:

```{r}
ref <- survival::coxph(survival::Surv(time, status) ~ age + bun, data = myeloma)
cbind(cox_fit = coef(fit), coxph = coef(ref))
```

## Empirical hazards

`emp_hazard()` estimates the hazard by a piecewise constant function: events
divided by the person-time at risk in each interval. Censored observations
contribute person-time but no event. This is the estimator used in the lectures
to show how a frailty model produces a decreasing population hazard even when
every individual has a constant hazard.

```{r}
emp_hazard(iud$time, breaks = seq(0, 130, by = 26), status = iud$status)
```

## Sample size and power for the log-rank test

`n_events_logrank()` gives the number of events required by Schoenfeld's
formula, and `power_logrank()` is the inverse calculation. Collett's worked
example compares a five-year survival of 0.41 with 0.60:

```{r}
hr <- log(0.60) / log(0.41)
hr
n_events_logrank(hr)
ceiling(n_events_logrank(hr))
power_logrank(d = 140, hr = 0.57)
```

`power_logrank_sim()` simulates trials with exponential survival times and
estimates the power by simulation instead, which is useful when proportional
hazards, no loss to follow-up or a fixed number of events cannot be assumed:

```{r}
power_logrank_sim(
  n = 400,
  hr = 0.57,
  lambda0 = -log(0.41) / 60,
  accrual = 18,
  followup = 24,
  nsim = 200,
  seed = 1
)
```

## Competing risks

`cif_cause_specific()` builds the cumulative incidence function for each cause
from cause-specific Cox models, with the other causes treated as censored:

```{r}
cause_specific <- list(
  thrombosis = survival::coxph(survival::Surv(time, cof == 2) ~ age, data = liver),
  other = survival::coxph(survival::Surv(time, cof == 4) ~ age, data = liver)
)
cif <- cif_cause_specific(
  cause_specific,
  newdata = data.frame(age = 60),
  times = c(365, 1825)
)
round(cif, 3)
```

The overall event-free survival that the integral is built on is attached to the
result:

```{r}
attr(cif, "survival")
```
